items.prompt: A student claims a coin is fair, but in 20 flips it landed heads 17 times. To test the claim, the student simulates 100 trials of 20 flips of a fair coin. Only 1 of the 100 trials produced 17 or more heads. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.answer: The result is rare under a fair-coin model, so the data are not consistent with it.

wrong.text: The result is possible with a fair coin, so the data prove that the coin is fair.
wrong.why: Treated 'possible' as 'likely'; ignored that 17 or more heads occurred in only 1% of simulated trials.

wrong.text: The result is above the expected 10 heads, so the simulation proves that the coin is unfair.
wrong.why: Treated any deviation from the expected count as proof; a simulation gives evidence, not certainty.

wrong.text: The result is consistent with a fair coin, because 17 of the 20 flips is more than half.
wrong.why: Confused 'more than half' with 'typical'; the simulation shows such a count is rare.

items.explanation: Under the fair-coin model, 17 or more heads happened in only 1 of 100 trials (1%). That is rare, so the observed result is not consistent with a fair coin.

items.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections, one of them red, so the model says P(red) = 1/4. In 40 real spins it landed on red 16 times. A simulation of 100 trials of 40 spins with P(red) = 1/4 gave 16 or more reds in 9 of the trials. Which statement is best?
items.answer: 16 or more reds happened in 9% of trials, so the data fit the model.

wrong.text: The expected number is 10 reds, so 16 reds shows that the spinner is not fair.
wrong.why: Compared the count to the expected value without using the simulation to judge how unusual it is.

wrong.text: The observed proportion is 16/40 = 2/5, so the model of 1/4 is certainly wrong.
wrong.why: Assumed any difference between observed and model proportions disproves the model.

wrong.text: The simulation proves that the spinner is fair and the model is exactly right.
wrong.why: Claimed a simulation can prove a model true; it can only show consistency.

items.explanation: A result at least as extreme as 16 reds occurred in 9 of 100 simulated trials, which is not unusual. The data do not contradict the 1/4 model, though they do not prove it.

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {4, 5}. What is P(A ∪ B)?

wrong.why: Added P(A) + P(B) = 3/6 + 2/6 and counted the shared outcome 4 twice.
Found P(A ∩ B), the single shared outcome, instead of the union.
Found the probability of outcomes in neither event, the complement of A ∪ B.

items.explanation: A ∪ B = {2, 4, 5, 6}, which is 4 of the 6 outcomes, so P(A ∪ B) = 4/6 = 2/3.

items.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Let A = the sum is 7 and B = at least one die shows a 3. What is P(A ∩ B)?

wrong.why: Used P(A) = 6/36 alone and ignored the requirement that a 3 also appears.
Used P(B) = 11/36 alone and ignored the requirement that the sum is 7.
Computed P(A | B) by dividing by the 11 outcomes in B instead of the 36 in the sample space.

items.explanation: Outcomes with sum 7 and a 3 are (3, 4) and (4, 3). That is 2 of the 36 equally likely outcomes, so P(A ∩ B) = 2/36 = 1/18.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. Which statement is correct?
items.answer: A and B are independent, because 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3.

wrong.text: A and B are not independent, because 0.6 + 0.5 ≠ 0.3.
wrong.why: Compared P(A ∩ B) with the sum of the probabilities; independence uses the product.

wrong.text: A and B are not independent, because P(A ∩ B) is less than P(B).
wrong.why: Believed independent events must have P(A ∩ B) equal to one of the single probabilities.

wrong.text: A and B are mutually exclusive, because 0.3 is less than both probabilities.
wrong.why: Confused independence with mutual exclusivity; mutually exclusive events would have P(A ∩ B) = 0.

items.explanation: Events are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Here 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3, which matches P(A ∩ B), so they are independent.

items.prompt: Events A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.12. Find P(B | A). Give a fraction or decimal.
items.explanation: Since A and B are independent, P(B | A) = P(B). P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), so P(B) = 0.12 ÷ 0.4 = 0.3 = 3/10.

wrong.why: Gave P(A ∩ B) instead of dividing by P(A).
Gave P(A); P(B | A) is P(B), not P(A).

items.prompt: A survey of 150 students recorded grade level and whether each plays a school sport. Grade 10: 45 play a sport and 35 do not. Grade 11: 30 play a sport and 40 do not. What is P(plays a sport | grade 11)?

wrong.why: Divided 30 by the grand total 150 instead of the 70 grade 11 students.
Divided 30 by the 75 students who play a sport, which finds P(grade 11 | plays a sport).
Divided 30 by 80, the number of grade 10 students, using the wrong row total.

items.explanation: Restrict to the 70 grade 11 students (30 + 40). Of those, 30 play a sport, so the probability is 30/70 = 3/7.

items.prompt: Students at a school were asked how they get to school. Girls: 24 take the bus and 16 walk. Boys: 18 take the bus and 22 walk. A student who walks is chosen at random. What is the probability the student is a girl? Give a fraction or a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
items.explanation: There are 16 + 22 = 38 students who walk, and 16 of them are girls. So P(girl | walks) = 16/38 = 8/19.

wrong.why: Divided 16 by the 40 girls, finding P(walks | girl).
Divided 16 by the grand total 80 instead of the 38 who walk.

items.prompt: Of 100 students, 30 are left-handed and 70 are right-handed. Among the left-handed students, 6 wear glasses. Among the right-handed students, 14 wear glasses. Which statement is correct?
items.answer: They are independent, because P(glasses | left-handed) = P(glasses) = 1/5.

wrong.text: They are not independent, because 6 and 14 are different counts.
wrong.why: Compared raw counts from groups of different sizes instead of comparing probabilities.

wrong.text: They are not independent, because fewer left-handed students wear glasses.
wrong.why: Used the count of left-handed glasses wearers; the group is smaller, so the count says nothing about independence.

wrong.text: They are independent, because 6 + 14 = 20 students wear glasses overall.
wrong.why: Found the total number wearing glasses but never compared it with the conditional probability.

items.explanation: P(glasses) = 20/100 = 1/5 and P(glasses | left-handed) = 6/30 = 1/5. The two probabilities are equal, so the events are independent.

items.prompt: A survey asked students in two groups whether they own a bike. Group X: 18 yes, 12 no. Group Y: some number of yes answers and 28 no. The survey results show that owning a bike and group are independent. How many students in Group Y answered yes?
items.explanation: Independence means P(yes | X) = P(yes | Y). P(yes | X) = 18/30 = 3/5, so P(no | Y) = 2/5. Then 28 is 2/5 of Group Y, so Group Y has 70 students and 70 − 28 = 42 answered yes.

wrong.why: Copied the no count instead of finding the yes count.
Assumed both groups must have the same number of yes answers.

items.prompt: In a survey of 80 students, 45 are girls and 35 are boys. A total of 32 students take Spanish, and 20 of those are girls. If you build a two-way frequency table of gender by Spanish, how many boys do not take Spanish?

wrong.why: Found the number of boys who do take Spanish, not those who do not.
Found the number of girls who do not take Spanish.
Subtracted 32 from 45, mixing the girls total with the Spanish total.

items.explanation: Boys taking Spanish = 32 − 20 = 12. Boys not taking Spanish = 35 − 12 = 23.

items.prompt: A two-way table of 200 students shows year and whether they have a job. Juniors: 50 with a job, 60 without. Seniors: 70 with a job, 20 without. In the table of relative frequencies (each count divided by the grand total), what value goes in the cell for seniors with a job?

wrong.why: Divided 70 by the 120 students with a job, giving a conditional frequency.
Divided 70 by the 90 seniors, giving a conditional frequency.
Read the juniors-without-a-job cell, 60 out of 200.

items.explanation: A relative frequency cell is the count divided by the grand total: 70/200 = 7/20 = 35%.

items.prompt: Of 200 people surveyed, 60% subscribe to a streaming service. One third of the subscribers are under 18, and one fourth of the non-subscribers are under 18. How many of the 200 people are under 18?

wrong.why: Counted only the under-18 subscribers and skipped the non-subscribers.
Took 1/4 of all 200 people, ignoring the different rates in each group.
Used the number of non-subscribers instead of the under-18 count.

items.explanation: Subscribers: 0.6 × 200 = 120, and 1/3 of them is 40. Non-subscribers: 80, and 1/4 of them is 20. Total under 18 = 40 + 20 = 60.

items.prompt: At one school, P(late | rainy morning) = 0.20, while P(late) = 0.08 over all mornings. Which is the best interpretation?
items.answer: Students are more often late on rainy mornings: 20% then, versus 8% overall.

wrong.text: Of all the students who are late, 20% were late on a rainy morning.
wrong.why: Reversed the condition, reading P(late | rainy) as P(rainy | late).

wrong.text: Rain causes 20% of all students to be late for school on every rainy day.
wrong.why: Read a conditional probability as proof of cause; it only shows an association.

wrong.text: On 20% of all mornings it rains and some students are late for school.
wrong.why: Read the conditional probability as a joint probability P(rainy and late).

items.explanation: P(late | rainy morning) restricts attention to rainy mornings only: 20% of students are late then, compared with 8% on all mornings. It describes association, not cause.

items.prompt: Which statement says in everyday language that owning a pet and being in the school orchestra are independent?
items.answer: Orchestra members own pets at the same rate as all students overall.

wrong.text: No student is both a pet owner and also an orchestra member.
wrong.why: Described mutually exclusive events (P(A ∩ B) = 0), not independent events.

wrong.text: Orchestra members are more likely than other students to own a pet.
wrong.why: Described a positive association, which is the opposite of independence.

wrong.text: There are about as many pet owners as there are orchestra members.
wrong.why: Compared the sizes of the two groups; independence compares rates, not group sizes.

items.explanation: Independence means knowing a student is in the orchestra does not change the chance they own a pet: P(pet | orchestra) = P(pet).

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Given that the result is greater than 2, what is the probability that it is even?

wrong.why: Used P(even and greater than 2) = 2/6, without dividing by P(greater than 2).
Found P(greater than 2 | even) = 2/3, reversing the condition.
Counted only one favorable outcome out of the 6 on the die.

items.explanation: Given the result is in {3, 4, 5, 6}, 2 of those 4 outcomes (4 and 6) are even. So P = 2/4 = 1/2.

items.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum is 8, what is the probability that at least one die shows a 6?

wrong.why: Found P(sum is 8 and a 6) over all 36 outcomes instead of only the outcomes with sum 8.
Found P(at least one 6) and ignored the given information.
Reversed the condition, dividing by the 11 outcomes that contain a 6.

items.explanation: Sum 8 gives (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): 5 outcomes. Two contain a 6, so the probability is 2/5.

items.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. Given that at least one flip is heads, what is the probability that exactly two flips are heads?

wrong.why: Divided by all 8 outcomes instead of only the 7 outcomes with at least one head.
Found P(at least one head) instead of the conditional probability.
Divided by 6, counting only outcomes with one or two heads and dropping HHH.

items.explanation: Outcomes with at least one head: 7. Those with exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH = 3. So P = 3/7.

items.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 play an instrument. Of those 18 students, 12 also sing in the chorus. What is the probability that a student who plays an instrument also sings in the chorus? Give a fraction or a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
items.explanation: Restrict to the 18 instrument players. Of these, 12 sing in the chorus, so the probability is 12/18 = 2/3.

wrong.why: Divided 12 by the whole class of 30.
Gave the count instead of a probability.

items.prompt: In a school, 40% of students take art, 50% take music, and 25% take both. A student who takes art is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student also takes music?

wrong.why: Divided 25% by the music percentage, finding P(art | music) instead.
Gave P(art and music) without dividing by P(art).
Divided the art percentage by the music percentage.

items.explanation: P(music | art) = P(art and music) ÷ P(art) = 0.25 ÷ 0.40 = 5/8.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.40, P(B) = 0.35, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.15. What is P(A ∪ B)?

wrong.why: Added P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap.
Added P(A) + P(B) + P(A ∩ B) instead of subtracting the overlap.
Multiplied P(A) × P(B), a rule for intersections of independent events, not for a union.

items.prompt: One card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck (13 hearts, and 12 face cards: J, Q, K in each of 4 suits). What is the probability that the card is a heart or a face card?

wrong.why: Added 13/52 + 12/52 and counted the 3 hearts that are face cards twice.
Found P(heart and face card), the overlap, instead of the union.
Subtracted the overlap twice, 25/52 − 6/52.

items.explanation: There are 3 face cards that are hearts. P(heart or face) = 13/52 + 12/52 − 3/52 = 22/52 = 11/26.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.55, P(A ∪ B) = 0.80, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.20. Find P(B). Give a fraction or a decimal.

wrong.why: Computed 0.80 − 0.55 and forgot to add back the overlap.
Rearranged the addition rule incorrectly, computing 0.80 + 0.55 − 0.20.

items.prompt: Of 100 students, 50 play a sport, 40 play an instrument, and 15 do both. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student does neither?

wrong.why: Subtracted 50 + 40 from 100, forgetting that the 15 who do both were counted twice.
Found the probability of doing at least one activity instead of neither.
Found the probability of playing a sport but not an instrument.

items.explanation: At least one: 50 + 40 − 15 = 75 students. Neither: 100 − 75 = 25, so P = 25/100 = 1/4.

items.prompt: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. What is P(A | B)?

wrong.why: Found P(B | A) = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 instead, dividing by the wrong event.
Found P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 and stopped without dividing by P(B).
Divided P(B) by P(A ∪ B) = 0.7, which is not a conditional probability of A given B.

items.prompt: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?

wrong.why: Treated the draws as independent with 5/8 each time, as if the marble was replaced.
Used 5/8 × 4/8, forgetting to reduce the denominator after the first draw.
Used 5/8 × 5/7, reducing the denominator but not the number of red marbles.

items.explanation: P(first red) = 5/8. With one red gone, P(second red | first red) = 4/7. Then 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

items.prompt: Two cards are dealt one after the other, without replacement, from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces?

wrong.why: Treated the draws as independent, using 4/52 × 4/52.
Used 4/52 × 3/52, reducing the aces but not the number of cards left.
Used 4/52 × 1/51, using 1 ace instead of 3 for the second draw.

items.explanation: P(first ace) = 4/52. With one ace gone, P(second ace | first ace) = 3/51. Then 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.

items.prompt: A box contains 6 green and 4 yellow marbles. Two marbles are drawn one after the other without replacement. What is the probability that the first is green and the second is yellow? Give a fraction or a decimal rounded to the nearest thousandth.
items.explanation: P(green first) = 6/10. Then 9 marbles remain, 4 yellow, so P(yellow | green) = 4/9. P = 6/10 × 4/9 = 24/90 = 4/15.

wrong.why: Used 6/10 × 4/10, as if the first marble was replaced.
Used only P(yellow) = 4/10 and ignored the first draw.

items.prompt: A box has 4 red and 6 white marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is red?

wrong.why: Found the probability that neither is red, the complement.
Found the probability that both are red, 4/10 × 3/9.
Added 4/10 + 4/9 instead of using the multiplication rule and the complement.

items.explanation: P(no red) = 6/10 × 5/9 = 1/3. So P(at least one red) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.

items.prompt: A jar holds 5 red, 4 blue, and 3 green marbles. Three marbles are drawn one after another without replacement. What is the probability of drawing red, then blue, then green in that order?

wrong.why: Treated the draws as independent, using 5/12 × 4/12 × 3/12.
Multiplied by 6 to allow any order, but the question asks for one specific order.
Multiplied only the first two draws and left out the green marble.

items.explanation: 5/12 × 4/11 × 3/10 = 60/1320 = 1/22, since the denominator and the matching color count drop after each draw.
